questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 4 day history of cough productive of green sputum, fever and right-sided chest pain that is worse on deep inspiration. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There are crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Productive cough, fever and pleuritic pain with focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds is pneumonia. Acute bronchitis has no bronchial breathing.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base
steps.x: Infective symptoms plus **pleuritic pain** and a **focal** area of **bronchial breathing** = consolidated lung.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An LRTI of the lung parenchyma: pneumonia.

elim: Bronchitis does not give bronchial breath sounds; they point to consolidated lung.
PE gives pleuritic pain and breathlessness but not green sputum with focal crackles and bronchial breathing.
Pneumothorax gives reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance, not crackles and fever.
LVF gives bibasal fine crackles and frothy sputum without fever or a focal bronchial area.

steps.x: **C. Community-acquired pneumonia.** Bronchial breath sounds are the sign that separates pneumonia from bronchitis.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man attends his GP with a 6 day history of cough productive of clear then yellow sputum after a cold. He feels tired but is not breathless. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. There are scattered wheezes that clear with coughing. There are no crackles or bronchial breath sounds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An LRTI of the bronchi after a viral cold with no crackles, no bronchial breathing and normal saturations is acute bronchitis, usually viral.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: no crackles or bronchial breath sounds
steps.x: Cough and sputum but a **normal chest** apart from wheeze that clears, and **normal saturations**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inflammation of the bronchi, not the alveoli: acute bronchitis.

elim: No history of atopy or variable wheeze; the wheeze is transient and the illness followed a cold.
Bronchiectasis is chronic daily sputum over months, not a 6 day illness.
Pneumonia would give focal crackles or bronchial breathing and often low saturations.
Abscess gives foul sputum, swinging fevers and a cavity; this is a mild short illness.

steps.x: **A. Acute bronchitis.** LRTI includes bronchitis (bronchi) and pneumonia (parenchyma); no bronchial breathing means no consolidation.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a 2 day history of high fever, rigors and cough productive of rust-coloured sputum. He has COPD. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows dense consolidation confined to the left lower lobe.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Sudden high fever, rusty sputum and lobar consolidation is classic pneumococcal pneumonia; S. pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of LRTI.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: confined to the left lower lobe
steps.x: Abrupt onset, **rusty sputum** and a **single lobe** consolidated in a man with **COPD**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The most common bacterial cause: pneumococcus.

elim: Klebsiella is rare, typically in alcohol dependence with upper lobe 'redcurrant jelly' sputum.
Legionella follows water-system exposure and gives diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and confusion.
Mycoplasma affects younger people with a gradual dry cough and patchy changes.
S. aureus pneumonia classically follows influenza and causes cavitation.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pneumoniae.** Unless the stem points elsewhere (travel, post-flu, alcohol), the organism is Streptococcus pneumoniae.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has her third chest infection this year. She takes methotrexate and prednisolone 10 mg daily. She has never smoked and drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Her temperature is 38.1°C and there are crackles at the left base.
questions.q: Which factor in her history most increases her risk of lower respiratory tract infection?
questions.e: Methotrexate and long-term prednisolone suppress immunity, a key risk factor for LRTI alongside smoking and COPD.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Recurrent infections in a non-smoker on **methotrexate and steroids**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Risk factors: smoking, COPD, immunosuppression. She only has the last.

elim: 4 units a week is within safe limits and is not a meaningful risk.
Calcium channel blockers do not increase infection risk.
Sex is not a recognised risk factor for LRTI.
Hypertension does not predispose to chest infection.

steps.x: **E. Immunosuppressive medication.** Smoking, COPD and immunosuppression are the risk factors to look for in the history.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a 3 week history of cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, swinging fevers and weight loss. He drinks 80 units of alcohol a week and has several broken, decayed teeth. There are coarse crackles over the right mid zone. A chest X-ray (see item resources) is shown.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Thick-walled cavity in the right mid zone with an air-fluid level.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Foul sputum, fevers, alcohol dependence and poor dentition with a cavity on X-ray is a lung abscess from anaerobic aspiration.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Foul sputum = **anaerobes**; alcohol + **poor dentition** = aspiration risk; the X-ray shows a cavity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Necrosis of lung parenchyma walled off into a cavity: lung abscess.

elim: Cancer can cavitate, but foul sputum and swinging fever with poor dentition and alcohol point to abscess.
Empyema is pus in the pleural space, seen as an effusion, not an intrapulmonary cavity.
TB cavities are usually apical with night sweats; foul-smelling sputum suggests anaerobes.
Sarcoid gives bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, not a cavity with foul sputum.

steps.x: **C. Lung abscess.** Alcohol + bad teeth + foul sputum + cavity = lung abscess.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman is admitted with a 3 day history of productive cough and fever. Today she is drowsy and has not passed urine for 12 hours. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. There are crackles at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Pneumonia with hypotension, tachycardia, drowsiness and oliguria is sepsis, an emergency requiring admission.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Infection plus **hypotension**, **oliguria** and **reduced consciousness** = organ dysfunction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: LRTI complicated by sepsis.

elim: Pulmonary oedema gives bibasal crackles and a raised JVP, not fever with hypotension.
Abscess develops over weeks with foul sputum; it does not explain shock today.
An effusion gives stony dullness and reduced breath sounds, not hypotension and oliguria.
There is no sudden pain or hyper-resonance; this is circulatory failure from infection.

steps.x: **E. Sepsis.** Respiratory failure, sepsis and effusion are the complications; hypotension and confusion mean sepsis.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with right lower lobe pneumonia becomes more breathless on the ward. He is alert. His respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. An arterial blood gas is taken on air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: PaO2 below 8 kPa with a normal or low PaCO2 is type 1 respiratory failure, a recognised complication of pneumonia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Low **PaO2** with a **low PaCO2** as he hyperventilates.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hypoxaemia without hypercapnia: type 1 respiratory failure.

elim: His CO2 is low, not raised, so this is not respiratory acidosis.
pH is high and bicarbonate normal; there is no metabolic acidosis.
PaO2 of 7.2 kPa is well below 8 kPa: he is in respiratory failure.
Type 2 needs a raised PaCO2 (>6.0 kPa); his is 4.1 kPa.

steps.x: **D. Type 1 respiratory failure.** PaO2 <8 kPa: type 1 if CO2 normal or low, type 2 if CO2 high.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man sees his GP with a 4 day history of productive cough, fever and fatigue. His daughter says that since this morning he has been muddled and thought she was his sister. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There are crackles at the right base.
questions.q: Which feature most indicates that he needs hospital admission?
questions.e: Hypoxia, confusion or sepsis are emergency features of LRTI needing admission; new confusion also scores on CURB-65.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: muddled and thought she was his sister
steps.x: Observations are stable but he is **newly confused**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The red flag here is confusion.

elim: Focal crackles confirm the LRTI but do not by themselves mean admission.
Fatigue is a common, non-specific feature of LRTI.
Productive cough is the usual presentation, not an emergency feature.
Fever is expected; his other observations are stable.

steps.x: **C. New confusion.** Hypoxia, confusion or sepsis = admit. Confusion is the C of CURB-65.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has a 3 day history of fever, cough productive of yellow sputum and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Her chest X-ray (see item resources) is shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Focal airspace opacification in the left lower zone with infective symptoms is consolidation from pneumonia; chest X-ray is the diagnostic test.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Infective symptoms with **left-sided pleuritic pain** and a single-zone opacity on X-ray.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Consolidation on CXR confirms pneumonia.

elim: Collapse shows volume loss and a sail sign, usually without fever over 3 days.
An effusion shows a meniscus blunting the costophrenic angle, not airspace shadowing.
Pneumothorax shows a visible lung edge with no markings beyond it.
Oedema is bilateral perihilar shadowing, not a single lobe.

steps.x: **B. Left lower lobe pneumonia.** Chest X-ray confirming consolidation is the diagnostic test for pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has a 5 day history of productive cough, fever and right-sided chest pain. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows right middle lobe consolidation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the right chest?
o: Absent breath sounds with stony dullness
questions.e: Consolidated lung is filled with exudate that conducts sound, giving crackles and bronchial breathing, often with increased vocal resonance and dullness.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Consolidation is **solid, airless** lung that **transmits** sound well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Crackles plus bronchial breathing over the consolidated lobe.

elim: This is a pleural effusion, not consolidation.
This is pneumothorax.
Consolidation changes the breath sounds; a normal chest suggests bronchitis.
Deviation towards a lesion suggests collapse with volume loss, not consolidation.

steps.x: **B. Crackles with bronchial breath sounds.** Consolidation: dull, crackles, bronchial breathing. Effusion: stony dull, absent sounds.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man is seen in the Emergency Department with a 3 day history of productive cough, fever and breathlessness. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Crackles and bronchial breath sounds are heard at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Examination has found focal signs; chest X-ray confirming consolidation is the gold-standard diagnostic test for pneumonia.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.

clues: Crackles and bronchial breath sounds are heard at the left base
steps.x: Examination has already been done and shows **focal signs**: now confirm consolidation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chest X-ray.

elim: CTPA is for suspected PE; this is infection with focal signs.
CRP shows inflammation but cannot confirm consolidation.
Spirometry assesses obstructive disease, not acute infection.
Culture identifies the organism later but does not diagnose pneumonia.

steps.x: **B. Chest X-ray.** Examine first, then confirm consolidation on chest X-ray.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She is alert and orientated. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 126/74 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. She has no allergies. Investigations: urea 8.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.8).
questions.q: Which is her CURB-65 score?
questions.e: Urea >7 mmol/L (1) and age ≥65 (1) give CURB-65 of 2: moderate severity under the NICE/BTS assessment.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Go through **C, U, R, B, 65** one at a time.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confusion 0, Urea 1, RR 0, BP 0, Age 1 = 2.

elim: She scores for both age and urea.
Age 65 or over scores 1, and urea >7 mmol/L scores another.
She is not confused, RR is under 30 and BP is above 90/60.
Only two criteria are met.

steps.x: **C. 2.** CURB-65: Confusion, Urea >7, RR ≥30, BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, age ≥65. 2 = moderate.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with alcohol dependence has a 2 week history of fevers and cough productive of large amounts of foul-smelling sputum. He was found unconscious after a binge 3 weeks ago. His temperature is 38.5°C and there are coarse crackles at the right base. A chest X-ray is requested.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
o: Lung edge with absent markings beyond
questions.e: Aspiration while unconscious leads to an anaerobic lung abscess, seen on X-ray as a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Aspiration while **unconscious** plus **foul sputum** = lung abscess.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A cavity containing pus and air.

elim: This suggests sarcoidosis.
This is pulmonary oedema.
This is a pleural effusion.
This is a pneumothorax.

steps.x: **D. Cavity with an air-fluid level.** Lung abscess on CXR: cavity with an air-fluid level.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a 3 day history of productive cough, fever and breathlessness on minimal exertion. She is alert. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Crackles are heard at the right base. She is lying flat and looks cyanosed around the lips.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Reduced oxygen saturation is a feature of LRTI; checking saturations first decides whether she needs oxygen now.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
She looks **hypoxic**: her saturation is the missing observation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Measure oxygen saturation.

elim: Useful in admitted patients, but they will not guide her immediate oxygen needs.
CT is not an initial test in suspected pneumonia.
There is no effusion to tap.
Culture takes days and does not affect immediate care.

steps.x: **D. Pulse oximetry.** Hypoxia is an emergency feature; measure saturations and give oxygen if low.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant has a 3 day history of productive cough and fever. She had an anaphylactic reaction to penicillin as a child. She is alert. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. There are crackles at the left base. Her CURB-65 score is 0.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: No antibiotics and review in 1 week
questions.e: Mild pneumonia in penicillin allergy is treated with doxycycline or clarithromycin; in pregnancy clarithromycin is chosen as doxycycline is avoided.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
**Mild**, **penicillin allergic** and **pregnant**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Use the penicillin-allergy alternative that is safe in pregnancy.

elim: She has had anaphylaxis to penicillin.
Co-amoxiclav contains a penicillin.
Doxycycline is a penicillin-allergy option but tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy.
Crackles and fever mean pneumonia, which needs antibiotics.

steps.x: **C. Oral clarithromycin.** Mild LRTI: amoxicillin; penicillin allergy: doxycycline or clarithromycin (clarithromycin if pregnant).

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is admitted with a 4 day history of productive cough and fever. He is alert and orientated. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. He has no allergies. A chest X-ray shows right lower zone consolidation. His urea is 8.2 mmol/L (2.5–7.8).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: Moderate community-acquired pneumonia needing admission is treated with amoxicillin plus clarithromycin to cover atypical organisms; severe disease escalates to co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin.

steps.x: A management question about which antibiotics: grade the severity first.
Urea and age score, nothing else: CURB-65 **2**, moderate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Moderate disease: amoxicillin plus a macrolide.

elim: Monotherapy is for mild disease; urea and age give him a CURB-65 of 2.
This is reserved for severe disease (CURB-65 3–5).
Doxycycline is the penicillin-allergy option for mild disease.
Broad-spectrum carbapenems are not used for community-acquired pneumonia.

steps.x: **B. Amoxicillin plus clarithromycin.** Mild: amoxicillin. Moderate: amoxicillin + clarithromycin. Severe: co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman is admitted with pneumonia. She is confused. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Investigations: urea 11.2 mmol/L (2.5–7.8). She has no drug allergies. Oxygen and intravenous fluids have been started.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: CURB-65 of 5 is severe pneumonia, treated with IV co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin alongside supportive care.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
Confusion, urea, RR, BP and age all score: **CURB-65 of 5**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe disease: IV co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin.

elim: Oral monotherapy is for mild disease; she scores 5 on CURB-65.
This is the moderate regimen; she is severe and septic.
Doxycycline is the mild-disease alternative in penicillin allergy.
Vancomycin is for MRSA, not standard community-acquired pneumonia.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin.** Severe (CURB-65 3–5): escalate to co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin, given IV.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man sees his GP with a 3 day history of cough productive of yellow sputum, fever and mild breathlessness. He has no allergies and no medical history. He is alert. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 130/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. On chest examination there are crackles at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Mild LRTI with focal signs in a well patient with no allergy is treated with oral amoxicillin in the community.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
Well, **no allergy**, CURB-65 **0**, focal crackles on examination.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mild disease: amoxicillin.

elim: Clarithromycin is the alternative in penicillin allergy; he has none.
Co-amoxiclav is for severe disease (with clarithromycin).
CURB-65 is 0 with normal saturations; he can be treated at home.
Focal crackles and fever suggest pneumonia, which needs antibiotics.

steps.x: **B. Oral amoxicillin for 5 days.** Mild LRTI and no allergy: amoxicillin.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with no lung disease is admitted with left lower lobe pneumonia and started on amoxicillin and clarithromycin. Two hours later she is more breathless. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Supportive care for LRTI includes oxygen if hypoxic; with no risk of CO2 retention, target 94–98%.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
Correct antibiotics already started; new problem is **saturation 89%**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Give oxygen.

elim: Antibiotics were only just started; the immediate problem is hypoxia.
There is no fluid overload; furosemide would worsen dehydration.
She has no wheeze or airways disease.
Steroids are not part of routine pneumonia care.

steps.x: **E. Oxygen to target saturation 94–98%.** Supportive care: oxygen if hypoxic, paracetamol for fever, fluids.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman sees her GP with a 3 day history of productive cough and fever. She is alert. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. There are crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Oral amoxicillin and review in 48 hours
questions.e: Hypoxia, confusion or sepsis in LRTI are emergency features requiring hospital admission; saturations of 88% need oxygen and admission.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
Not confused, but **saturation 88%**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hypoxia means hospital.

elim: A follow-up film is not the priority; she is hypoxic now.
She is hypoxic, which is an emergency feature needing admission.
She is not penicillin allergic and needs admission.
Results take days; hypoxia needs treatment today.

steps.x: **A. Arrange hospital admission.** Hypoxia, confusion or sepsis = admit, even if CURB-65 is low.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has had a cough productive of yellow sputum for 5 days. His chest is clear apart from wheeze and his chest X-ray is normal. His neighbour, aged 46, has similar symptoms but also has bronchial breath sounds at the right base and right lower lobe consolidation.
questions.q: Which site of inflammation best explains the difference between the two men?
o: Alveoli in the first, bronchi in the second
Bronchi in the first, alveoli in the second
Larynx in the first, bronchi in the second
Trachea in the first, pleura in the second
questions.e: LRTI involves the bronchi (bronchitis, normal X-ray) and/or the parenchyma (pneumonia, alveolar exudate giving consolidation and bronchial breathing).

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.

clues: bronchial breath sounds at the right base
steps.x: One has a **normal X-ray**; the other has **consolidation**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bronchitis vs pneumonia: bronchi vs alveoli.

elim: This is reversed: consolidation means alveoli are involved.
Laryngeal inflammation is an upper respiratory tract infection.
Pleural inflammation gives pleuritic pain and a rub, not consolidation.
Neither tracheitis nor pleurisy explains the X-ray findings.

steps.x: **B. Bronchi in the first, alveoli in the second.** Bronchitis = bronchi; pneumonia = alveolar exudate in the parenchyma.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man who smokes develops fever, rigors, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and cough productive of rusty sputum a week after a cold. His temperature is 39.0°C and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive diplococci. A chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route by which the organism reached his lungs?
o: Direct spread from a subphrenic abscess
Haematogenous spread from the heart valves
Reactivation of a latent primary infection
questions.e: Gram-positive diplococci are Streptococcus pneumoniae, which colonises the nasopharynx and descends into the lower respiratory tract.

steps.x: A science question about how the organism gets to the lung: identify the organism first.
**Gram-positive diplococci** = pneumococcus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pneumococcus colonises the nasopharynx first.

elim: There is no abdominal pathology.
That is septic emboli from right-sided endocarditis.
That is how Legionella is acquired.
That describes tuberculosis.

steps.x: **A. Descent from a colonised nasopharynx.** S. pneumoniae: nasopharyngeal coloniser that descends to the lungs.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman with alcohol dependence has a lung abscess in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. She has had several episodes of being found unconscious after drinking. Sputum smells foul. Her teeth are in good condition.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which her alcohol use caused the abscess?
o: Aspiration of oral flora during impaired consciousness
Direct toxic necrosis of lung by ethanol
questions.e: Impaired consciousness from alcohol allows aspiration of anaerobic oral flora, causing necrotising infection that walls off into a pus-filled cavity.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.

clues: posterior segment of the right upper lobe
steps.x: Unconscious episodes + **foul sputum** + a **dependent segment**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Aspiration of anaerobic oral flora.

elim: Ethanol does not directly necrose the lung.
Abscesses here are not spread from the liver.
Surfactant loss causes atelectasis, not a necrotising cavity.
Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke's, not abscess.

steps.x: **A. Aspiration of oral flora during impaired consciousness.** Lung abscess = aspiration of anaerobes when consciousness or swallowing is impaired.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man had a stroke 2 months ago and still coughs when drinking. He has severe gum disease and several rotten teeth. He now has a 3 week history of swinging fever and foul-smelling sputum. A chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe cavity with an air-fluid level.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason his dental disease increases his risk of this condition?
o: It allows bacteria to spread directly through the mediastinum
It causes bacteraemia that seeds the lung
It increases the anaerobic bacterial load available for aspiration
questions.e: Poor dentition increases the anaerobic load in the mouth, so that aspiration (here from post-stroke dysphagia) delivers more anaerobes, causing a necrotising abscess.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.
Dysphagia lets him **aspirate**; **rotten teeth** mean what he aspirates is full of anaerobes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: More anaerobes to aspirate.

elim: Spread is by aspiration, not direct extension.
Abscess here follows aspiration, not blood-borne seeding.
Teeth do not affect the cough reflex; his stroke does.
Saliva volume is not the mechanism.

steps.x: **D. It increases the anaerobic bacterial load available for aspiration.** Poor dentition = more anaerobic bacteria available for aspiration.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with alcohol dependence has a 4 week history of cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, night sweats and weight loss. He has very poor dentition. His temperature is 38.2°C. A chest X-ray shows a cavity with an air-fluid level in the apical segment of the right lower lobe.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism group?
questions.e: Foul-smelling sputum from a cavity in a patient with alcohol dependence and poor dentition is a lung abscess from aspirated anaerobic oral flora.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.
**Foul smell** is the giveaway for **anaerobes**; TB does not smell.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anaerobic oral flora.

elim: Mycoplasma and Chlamydophila cause atypical pneumonia, not abscess.
Aspergillus colonises existing cavities; it does not give foul sputum.
TB cavities are usually apical upper lobe with no foul smell; foul sputum points to anaerobes.
Viruses do not cause necrotising cavities.

steps.x: **A. Anaerobic oral bacteria.** Foul sputum = anaerobes = aspiration lung abscess.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman is on day 5 of oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin for left lower lobe pneumonia. She still has a fever and is more breathless. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. The left base is stony dull to percussion with absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Stony dullness, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance with persisting fever are a pleural effusion complicating pneumonia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
**Stony dull** with **reduced** vocal resonance means fluid, not consolidation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluid in the pleural space.

elim: Abscess gives a cavity and coarse crackles with foul sputum, not stony dullness.
Pneumothorax is hyper-resonant, not dull.
PE does not produce stony dullness with absent breath sounds.
Consolidation gives bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance, not reduced.

steps.x: **B. Pleural effusion.** Consolidation: increased vocal resonance. Effusion: stony dull, reduced vocal resonance.
